en.title: The new Halloween video game has been banned in Australia – and not because of the violence | Games
en.description: Academics and a former classification board director say Halloween: The Game’s ban due to ‘incentivised drug use’ highlights an incoherent set of s...
en.fullContent:
Academics and a former classification board director say Halloween: The Game’s ban due to ‘incentivised drug use’ highlights an incoherent set of standards

Halloween’s Michael Myers is one of film’s most feared boogeymen, responsible for some of the most brutal on-screen deaths in horror cinema. The US video game developer Illfonic looked to reproduce those terrors in its upcoming title Halloween: The Game, with gruesome killings a major focus of the gameplay: for instance, you can stomp another player’s head through a toilet seat, or fry their brain by throwing them through a television screen.

But Australians will not be able to play Halloween, because it has been refused classification by the Australian Classification Board, which means it is banned from sale within the country. And it’s not because of the violence or murders.

In the game, players can smoke marijuana to see the location of Michael Myers in order to avoid being killed – a use of drugs that the Classification Board has deemed a “gameplay advantage”. Under the Guidelines for the Classification of Computer Games 2023, video games are refused classification if they contain “illicit or proscribed drug use related to incentives or rewards”.

“Halloween: The Game contains illicit drug use that is linked to an incentive or reward, in that use of the drug provides a gameplay advantage to the player. It is on this basis that the game has been refused classification, as required under the Code and Guidelines,” the board wrote in a recent statement.

In the wake of the decision, Illfonic’s social media accounts have been flooded with comments from irate Australians. An FoI officer said the Classification Board had received more than 500 complaints in relation to Halloween: The Game.

en.title: "Forget trodden down, I think our future sees a beautiful revolution" - The people of video games on what gives them cause for hope
en.description: "Forget trodden down, I think our future sees a beautiful revolution."
en.fullContent:
"Forget trodden down, I think our future sees a beautiful revolution."

Hello and welcome to one of our final pieces for Optimism Week here on Eurogamer. This time, we've turned to the industry itself for some answers, and as such I'm going to do my best to get out of the way as quickly as possible.

For this piece, we contacted a range of developers and general people-of-video-games to ask them one question: despite everything, what still gives you reason for optimism?

As you'd expect, the responses have been wonderful. Here's why we should still be hopefully for the future of video games, straight from the people who make the medium possible:

"It's a rough time for the games industry but a golden age for the game dev community.

"I've seen a tremendous outpouring of support for people after layoffs and for new writers trying to break in. It's moving to see the way people rally around their colleagues to raise money, find jobs, offer feedback on resumes and portfolios.

en.title: CAA Launches Indie Game Acceleration Fund Frame1Games (EXCLUSIVE)
en.description: CAA has launched Frame1Games, a new venture to fund, accelerate and market independent video games.
en.fullContent:
CAA has launched Frame1Games, a new venture to fund, accelerate and market independent video games.

Per the agency, Frame1Games “pairs multi-million-dollar capital investment with a yearlong accelerator, giving developers mentorship from industry veterans and CAA executives and direct access to the partners and vendors needed to bring a game to market.”

CAA’s Frame1Games intends to back several independent projects each year with selected developers set to receive financing alongside strategic guidance across media, marketing, partnership, and distribution. Games included in the program will be showcased within a curated marketplace and, beginning in 2027, Frame1Games will support these titles at high-profile, consumer-facing video game industry events, including Summer Game Fest in June and The Game Awards in December.

Indie developers can apply to join Frame1Games’ first cohort at https://www.frame1games.com/.

Indie Fund investment partner Jared Yeager has been tapped to lead CAA’s Frame1Games. In his new role, Yeager, along with a board of experts, will oversee the program, advise participating developers, and build out the mentor network, “while cultivating strategic industry partnerships and guiding each cohort from development through commercialization.”

Along with his years spent as an investment partner with Indie Fund, which has backed more than 50 titles including “Hyper Light Drifter,” “Night in the Woods” and “Hollow Knight,” Yeager has spent 16 years as awards jury co-chair with IndieCade and is a founding member of FoxNext Games’ indie development fund. He has worked on major studio productions at Walt Disney Games, including “Avatar: Frontiers of Pandora.”

en.title: Trump's tariffs risk higher prices for AI, video games, cellphones: experts
en.description: From cellphones to gaming consoles and artificial intelligence infrastructure, experts say the escalating trade war between Canada and the United S...
en.fullContent:
From cellphones to gaming consoles and artificial intelligence infrastructure, experts say the escalating trade war between Canada and the United States will mean higher costs for consumers and businesses.

Canada exported more than $4 billion US worth of electronics equipment to the U.S. last year that would now be subject to U.S. President Donald Trump's new 50 per cent tariffs on a wide range of goods. Certain electrical boards and controllers represent the highest dollar value of any export category targeted by the new U.S. levies.

On Saturday, Prime Minister Mark Carney said Canada would match the Trump administration's tariffs dollar for dollar.

Experts say higher prices are a virtual certainty, as the escalating trade dispute threatens businesses on both sides of the border.

Carol McGlogan is president and CEO of Electro-Federation Canada, an industry group representing more than 230 companies in Canada's electrical and automation sector.

"The 50 per cent tariffs are devastating," she said on Monday, adding that 90 per cent of her member's exports go to the U.S.

en.title: Florida to ban video games and theme park tickets purchases with welfare assistance
en.description: TALLAHASSEE, Fla. — Florida plans to restrict how families can use Temporary Cash Assistance benefits, including prohibiting purchases of video gam...
en.fullContent:
TALLAHASSEE, Fla. — Florida plans to restrict how families can use Temporary Cash Assistance benefits, including prohibiting purchases of video games, theme park tickets, tattoos and several other products and services.

Gov. Ron DeSantis announced Monday that the state will amend its Temporary Assistance for Needy Families plan. The governor’s office said Florida will be the first state to impose these restrictions.

Under the amended plan, Temporary Cash Assistance benefits may not be used to directly purchase:

“Taxpayer-funded assistance should help families put food on the table, keep the lights on, purchase clothing, provide for their children and overcome barriers on the path toward independence,” DeSantis said in a statement.

Temporary Cash Assistance is issued through an EBT card and is intended to help eligible families pay for basic needs such as food, clothing, housing, utilities, household goods and personal care. According to the governor’s office, participating households receive an average of approximately $250 per month.

These cash benefits are separate from Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program benefits, commonly known as SNAP.
